rv.q: In holding up a dark funhouse mirror to the brutal extremes of Black life, Nwandu’s play transcends its theatrical form to become a poetic meditation that almost defies classification.

What makes Pass Over liberatingly unstable is the utter freedom with which Nwandu navigates moral and aesthetic categories, gliding from urban comedy to horror movie and finally (no spoilers) to a transcendent, Edenic release from reality.

At 95 minutes — roughly half the length of Samuel Beckett’s masterpiece — the play is a smart, sleek commentary on being young and Black and craving the peace of mind that comes with not feeling there’s a target on your back.
You can actually hear how hard it is for Nwandu to build up joy, because the new section is so transparent about its aesthetic effort.
Without ever forgetting its origin in American racism, “Pass Over” broadens to include every kind of -ism, including the ultimately unanswerable one of existentialism.
Essiedu rises up to his full potential: light on his feet one moment, walking as if his boots were filled with lead the next.
This urgent and provocative work is sometimes on-the-nose, a firm whack on the nose might be what the current Broadway moment demands.
This playwright's voice can be a joy to hear, and her language is often blistering.

“Pass Over” is no longer just an expression of authorial fury at the killing of young Black men by the police but a play that embraces intersectionality and says, in essence, that we all need to start over and recalibrate.

The play, a canny, streetwise meld of Beckett and the Bible suffused with magic realism and even an apparent fondness for ’70s sitcom The Jeffersons and its famous “Movin’ On Up” theme song, does indeed reflect this moment in time.
“Pass Over” is a compelling, if flawed, way to start things off in Times Square.
Pass Over is the embodiment of that change.
To watch them work together is a joy in itself.

The standing ovation, the whooping and cheering happened before a word was spoken. Pass Over opened tonight, August 22 (until Oct 10 at the Theatre), the first release on a pent-up Broadway itching to make up for a lost year and a half. Here we all were in what looked like a full house, and it felt momentous and strange.
Nwandu's play is a powerful piece of theater
Pass Over does not let any of us off the hook; we are all standing on that concrete block, these issues affect all of us.
In one sense, the show has gone Broadway.

The three actors, repeating their Lincoln Center performances, couldn't be better. Hill and Smallwood expertly play off each in the manner of seasoned vaudevillians, while Ebert delivers a tour-de-force turn, infused with comic physicality and an undercurrent of danger, that keeps us on edge even as we're laughing.
It remains, as she told the Times, “a lament.”
Because of course traumatic violence must appear––for all its sharp performances and often brilliant depiction of Black hope and hopelessness, little happens that can’t be seen from a mile away.
Pass Over raises several difficult issues and addresses them with humor, pathos, and ingenuity.

“Pass Over” is not for everyone – or even most people – but it is for those who are ready and willing to take in a raw, incendiary, and challenging (though often entertaining and gripping) piece of contemporary theater.

Vaxxine-verified and masked for protection from one ongoing societal scourge, Pass Over's audience bears witness to a powerful and timely indictment of another, one that’s equally dangerous yet more deeply entrenched.
I'd seen the show when it played at LCT3 in 2018 and I was knocked out by it.

cn.t: Critics praise this Beckett-inspired drama about two young Black men as powerful, timely, and darkly funny, though its allegorical approach occasionally overshadows character depth. A bold, provocative return for Broadway.
